claim: Xcr1+ dendritic cells are significantly more abundant in the plaque area of the human femoral artery compared to the plaque-free area.
source: As shown in Figure 1A and B, Xcr1+ dendritic cells were significantly more abundant in the plaque area of the human femoral artery compared to that in the plaque-free area.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical staining data from human femoral artery samples shown in Figure 1A and B, with quantitative analysis demonstrating statistical significance.

claim: Xcr1+CD11c+ dendritic cells accumulate in the plaques of the aortic root in Apoe–/– mice fed a high-fat diet for 16 weeks.
source: Similarly, the immunofluorescence staining results using specific antibodies for Xcr1 and CD11c revealed that Xcr1+CD11c+ dendritic cells accumulated in the plaques of the aortic root in Apoe–/– mice that were placed on a HFD for 16 weeks (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 1C and D, demonstrating the presence and accumulation of Xcr1+CD11c+ cells in aortic plaques.

claim: Xcr1+ cDC1 cells continuously accumulate in the lesioned area as atherosclerosis progresses.
source: Quantitative analysis was conducted using image processing software, revealing a continuous accumulation of Xcr1+ cDC1 cells in the lesioned area as the disease progressed (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of immunohistochemical data from aortic root sections at different time points (8, 12, and 16 weeks on HFD), shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The expression of tdRFP is exclusively present in Xcr1+ cDC1 when mice are fed a HFD for 16 weeks in bone marrow transplanted mice.
source: Remarkably, we found that the expression of tdRFP was exclusively present in Xcr1+ cDC1 when mice were fed a HFD for 16 weeks in the bone marrow transplanted mice, and the Cre recombinase activity was not detectable in non-cDC1 cells (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometric analysis of bone marrow transplanted mice showing tdRFP expression only in cDC1 cells, as shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: GFP expression is stringently restricted to cDC1 cells in Xcr1Cre-Gfp Apoe–/– mice fed a HFD for 16 weeks.
source: As expected, we found that the GFP expression was stringently restricted to cDC1 cells (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometric analysis of pDC, cDC1, and cDC2 cells from the spleen, showing GFP expression only in cDC1 cells, as shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: There is a complete loss of GFP-positive cells and Xcr1+ cDC1 cells in Xcr1+ cDC1-depleted mice.
source: Strikingly, we observed a complete loss of GFP-positive cells and Xcr1+ cDC1 cells in Xcr1+ cDC1-depleted mice (Figure 2D and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometric analysis comparing Xcr1Cre-Gfp Rosa26LSL-DTA Apoe–/– mice with control mice, shown in Figure 2D and F.

claim: Cre recombinase activity is selectively confined to cDC1 cells with no leakiness observed in lineages other than the Xcr1+ cDC1 population.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that Cre recombinase activity was selectively confined to cDC1 cells, and no leakiness was observed in lineages other than the Xcr1+ cDC1 population.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple flow cytometry experiments showing tdRFP and GFP expression exclusively in cDC1 cells.

claim: The size of the lesion in both descending aorta and aortic root is significantly smaller in Xcr1Cre-Gfp Rosa26LSL-DTA Apoe–/– mice compared with Apoe–/– control mice.
source: The Oil Red O (ORO) staining results demonstrated that the size of the lesion in both descending aorta and aortic root was significantly smaller in Xcr1Cre-Gfp Rosa26LSL-DTA Apoe–/– mice compared with Apoe–/– control mice (12.82% vs 6.01% in descending aorta; 39.25% vs 33.57% in ORO-stained aortic root) (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Oil Red O staining and quantitative analysis of lesion areas in both descending aorta and aortic root, shown in Figure 3A-D.

claim: No significant differences are observed in the necrotic core area of the aortic root between Xcr1Cre-Gfp Rosa26LSL-DTA Apoe–/– mice and Apoe–/– control mice.
source: Interestingly, no significant differences were observed in the necrotic core area of the aortic root between Xcr1Cre-Gfp Rosa26LSL-DTA Apoe–/– mice and Apoe–/– control mice (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by H&E staining and quantitative analysis of necrotic core areas, shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: Comparable proportions of F4/80+ CD11b+ macrophages are found in the aorta between Xcr1Cre-Gfp Rosa26LSL-DTA Apoe–/– mice and Apoe–/– control mice.
source: Similarly, subsequent flow cytometry analyses and IHC results revealed comparable proportions of F4/80+ CD11b+ macrophages in the aorta, as well as similar percentages of CD68-positive macrophages in the aortic lesions between the two groups of mice (Figure 3G–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry and immunohistochemistry data showing no significant differences in macrophage populations, as shown in Figure 3G-J.

claim: No significant differences exist in body weight or levels of total cholesterol, triglycerides, low-density lipoprotein, and high-density lipoprotein between Xcr1Cre-Gfp Rosa26LSL-DTA Apoe–/– mice and Apoe–/– control mice.
source: Our results indicated no significant differences in body weight or levels of total cholesterol (TC), triglycerides (TG), low-density lipoprotein (LDL), and high-density lipoprotein (HDL) between the two groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements of body weight and serum lipid profiles, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Specific depletion of cDC1 attenuates atherogenesis without affecting lipid status or macrophagic accumulation in aortic lesions.
source: Taken together, these results suggested that specific depletion of cDC1 attenuated atherogenesis without affecting lipid status or macrophagic accumulation in aortic lesions.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the combined data showing reduced atherosclerosis but no changes in lipid profiles or macrophage numbers.

claim: There is a total absence of Xcr1+ cDC1 in the aorta, lymph nodes, and spleen in Xcr1Cre-Gfp Rosa26LSL-DTA Apoe–/– mice fed a HFD for 16 weeks.
source: In the Xcr1Cre-Gfp Rosa26LSL-DTA Apoe–/– mice that were fed a HFD for 16 weeks, we observed a total absence of Xcr1+ cDC1 in the aorta, lymph nodes, and spleen (Figure 4A-C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometric analysis of multiple organs showing complete depletion of cDC1 cells, as shown in Figure 4A-C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Neither the frequencies nor absolute counts of aortic CD4+ and CD8+ T cells differ significantly between Xcr1Cre-Gfp Rosa26LSL-DTA Apoe–/– mice and Apoe–/– control mice.
source: While neither the frequencies nor absolute counts of aortic CD4+ and CD8+ T cells differed significantly between the two groups of mice (Figure 4D–F), CD69 frequency and CD44 MFI (Mean Fluorescence Intensity), the T cell activation markers, were significantly reduced in both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells from Xcr1+ cDC1 depleted mice compared to controls (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometric analysis of T cell populations in the aorta, shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: CD69 frequency and CD44 MFI are significantly reduced in both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells from Xcr1+ cDC1 depleted mice compared to controls.
source: While neither the frequencies nor absolute counts of aortic CD4+ and CD8+ T cells differed significantly between the two groups of mice (Figure 4D–F), CD69 frequency and CD44 MFI (Mean Fluorescence Intensity), the T cell activation markers, were significantly reduced in both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells from Xcr1+ cDC1 depleted mice compared to controls (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometric analysis of T cell activation markers in the aorta, shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: Decreased frequencies of CD69+ T cells are only observed in aortic lesions but not in lymphoid organs in Xcr1+ cDC1 depleted mice.
source: Interestingly, such decreased frequencies of CD69+ T cells were only observed in aortic lesions but not in lymphoid organs such as lymph nodes and the spleen in the Xcr1+ cDC1 depleted mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–B and D-E).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometric analysis comparing T cell activation in different organs, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-B and D-E.

claim: The absolute numbers of CD8+ and CD4+ T cells are markedly reduced in the spleen but not in the lymph nodes in Xcr1Cre-Gfp Rosa26LSL-DTA Apoe–/– mice compared to Apoe–/– mice.
source: We further analyzed the absolute numbers of CD8+ and CD4+ T cells in the spleen and lymph nodes and found that the absolute numbers of CD8+ and CD4+ T cells were markedly reduced in the spleen but not in the lymph nodes in Xcr1Cre-Gfp Rosa26LSL-DTA Apoe–/– mice compared to those in Apoe–/– mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometric quantification of T cell numbers in lymphoid organs, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C and F.

claim: Absence of cDC1 results in reduced frequencies of CD8+ T cells in both spleen and lymph nodes in hyperlipidemic mice.
source: Absence of cDC1 also resulted in reduced frequencies of CD8+ T cells in both spleen and lymph nodes in hyperlipidemic mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometric analysis of T cell populations in lymphoid organs.

claim: The frequencies of CD44high CD62Llow activated memory cells within the CD8+ subsets in both the spleen and lymph nodes are significantly lower in Xcr1+ cDC1 depleted mice than in Apoe–/– control mice.
source: More importantly, the frequencies of CD44high CD62Llow activated memory cells within the CD8+ subsets in both the spleen and lymph nodes were significantly lower than those in the Apoe–/– control mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometric analysis of memory T cell populations in lymphoid organs, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A-D.

claim: In aortic plaques, Xcr1+ cDC1 cells are implicated in activating CD4+ and CD8+ T cells.
source: Our data indicate that in aortic plaques, Xcr1+ cDC1 cells are implicated in activating CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, and the loss of the cDC1 population led to a decreased absolute count of CD8+ T cells in the lymph nodes of HFD-treated mice.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed reduction in T cell activation markers when cDC1 cells are depleted.

claim: Flow cytometric analysis displays almost complete depletion of cDC1 cells in Apoe−/− recipient mice transplanted with Xcr1Cre-Gfp Rosa26LSL-DTA bone marrow.
source: Interestingly, flow cytometric analysis of the aorta displayed almost complete depletion of cDC1 cells in Apoe−/− recipient mice transplanted with Xcr1Cre-Gfp Rosa26LSL-DTA bone marrow mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometric analysis of aortic cells in bone marrow transplanted mice, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: No significant changes are observed in pDCs and CD64+ F4/80+ aortic macrophages in bone marrow transplanted mice with cDC1 depletion.
source: Strikingly we did not find observe significant changes in pDCs and CD64+ F4/80+ aortic macrophages (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometric analysis of other immune cell populations in the aorta, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Bone marrow transplantation experiments confirm the fidelity of Cre recombinase expression in cDC1 cells in mice.
source: Therefore, our bone marrow transplantation experiments further confirmed fidelity of the Cre recombinase expression in cDC1 cells in mice.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the bone marrow transplantation results showing specific depletion of cDC1 cells.

claim: cDC1 cells from the spleen and lymph nodes differ markedly in their distribution across clusters.
source: Interestingly, the Xcr1+ cDC1 cells from the spleen and lymph nodes displayed an obvious difference in their distribution, and aortic Xcr1+ cDC1 cells appeared more enriched in a few clusters (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data showing different cluster distributions, as shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: Aortic Xcr1+ cDC1 cells are enriched in a few clusters that express marker genes Ccr2, Sept3, and Cldnd1.
source: Therefore, our data suggest that Xcr1+ cDC1 cells from the spleen and lymph nodes can differ markedly in heterogeneity, and aortic Xcr1+ cDC1 cells are enriched in a few clusters that express marker genes, Ccr2, Sept3, and Cldnd1 (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing analysis identifying differentially expressed genes in aortic cDC1 cells.

claim: Xcr1+ cDC1 in the aorta originate from bone marrow.
source: Together, these data implied that Xcr1+ cDC1 in the aorta originate from bone marrow, and Xcr1+ cDC1 cells exhibit strong heterogeneity among aorta, spleen, and lymph nodes.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on bone marrow transplantation experiments showing complete depletion of aortic cDC1 when donor bone marrow lacks functional cDC1.

claim: Xcr1+ cDC1 cells exhibit strong heterogeneity among aorta, spleen, and lymph nodes.
source: Together, these data implied that Xcr1+ cDC1 in the aorta originate from bone marrow, and Xcr1+ cDC1 cells exhibit strong heterogeneity among aorta, spleen, and lymph nodes.
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data showing different cluster distributions and gene expression patterns across organs.

claim: The size of lesion at the descending aorta and aortic root is significantly smaller in Xcl1–/– Apoe–/– compared to Apoe–/– mice.
source: As shown in Figure 6A–D, the size of lesion at the descending aorta and aortic root was significantly smaller in Xcl1–/– Apoe–/– compared to that in Apoe–/– mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by Oil Red O staining and quantitative analysis of lesion areas, shown in Figure 6A-D.

claim: ORO staining of the liver, body weight and blood lipid profiles reveal no significant differences between Xcl1–/– Apoe–/– and Apoe–/– mice.
source: Importantly, ORO staining of the liver, body weight and blood lipid profiles revealed no significant differences between the two groups (Figure 6E–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements of liver lipid content, body weight, and serum lipid profiles, shown in Figure 6E-H.

claim: The percentage of CD68 positive macrophages in aortic lesion is similar between Xcl1–/– Apoe–/– and Apoe–/– mice.
source: Moreover, the IHC experiment result shows the percentage of CD68 positive macrophages in aortic lesion was similar between two groups (Figure 6I–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing no significant difference in macrophage content, as shown in Figure 6I-J.

claim: Both frequencies and absolute counts of Xcr1+ cDC1 cells in the aorta are significantly reduced in Xcl1–/– Apoe–/– mice compared to Apoe–/– mice.
source: The flow cytometric results illustrated that both frequencies and absolute counts of Xcr1+ cDC1 cells in the aorta were significantly reduced, but cDCs and cDC2 cells from Xcl1–/– Apoe–/– were comparable with that from Apoe–/– (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometric analysis of dendritic cell populations in the aorta, shown in Figure 7A-C.

claim: cDCs and cDC2 cells from Xcl1–/– Apoe–/– are comparable with those from Apoe–/– mice.
source: The flow cytometric results illustrated that both frequencies and absolute counts of Xcr1+ cDC1 cells in the aorta were significantly reduced, but cDCs and cDC2 cells from Xcl1–/– Apoe–/– were comparable with that from Apoe–/– (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometric analysis showing no significant differences in cDC and cDC2 populations, as shown in Figure 7A-C.

claim: CD69+ frequency and CD44 MFI remain comparable in both aortic CD4+ and CD8+ T cells between Xcl1–/– Apoe–/– and Apoe–/– mice.
source: Crucially, CD69+ frequency and CD44 MFI remained comparable in both aortic CD4+ and CD8+ T cells between two groups (Figure 7D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometric analysis of T cell activation markers, shown in Figure 7D-F.

claim: Aortic CD8+ T cells exhibit reduced frequency and absolute count in Xcl1–/– Apoe–/– mice versus controls.
source: However, aortic CD8+ T cells exhibited reduced frequency and absolute count, while CD4+ T cells showed increased frequency but unchanged counts in Xcl1–/– Apoe–/– mouse versus controls (Figure 7G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometric quantification of T cell populations in the aorta, shown in Figure 7G and H.

claim: CD4+ T cells show increased frequency but unchanged counts in Xcl1–/– Apoe–/– mice versus controls.
source: However, aortic CD8+ T cells exhibited reduced frequency and absolute count, while CD4+ T cells showed increased frequency but unchanged counts in Xcl1–/– Apoe–/– mouse versus controls (Figure 7G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometric quantification of T cell populations in the aorta, shown in Figure 7G and H.

claim: Xcl1 promotes atherosclerosis by recruiting Xcr1+ cDC1 cells and facilitating CD8+ T cell accumulation in lesions.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that Xcl1 promotes atherosclerosis by recruiting Xcr1+ cDC1 cells, and facilitating CD8+ T cell accumulation in lesions.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the combined data showing reduced atherosclerosis, decreased cDC1 cells, and reduced CD8+ T cells in Xcl1 knockout mice.

claim: Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory disease that affects the large and medium-sized arteries and is the leading cause of cardiovascular mortality and morbidity worldwide.
source: Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory disease that affects the large and medium-sized arteries, and it is the leading cause of cardiovascular mortality and morbidity worldwide (Björkegren and Lusis, 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Björkegren and Lusis, 2022.

claim: Lipid-laden phagocytes such as macrophages, along with lymphocytes and dendritic cells, accumulate in atherosclerotic plaques.
source: Atherosclerosis is a complex pathological process during which lipid-laden phagocytes such as macrophages, along with lymphocytes and dendritic cells, accumulate in the plaque (Hansson and Hermansson, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hansson and Hermansson, 2011.

claim: Both innate and adaptive immunity are involved in the development of atherosclerosis.
source: Mounting evidence from animal models and human studies demonstrates involvement of both the innate and adaptive immunity in the development of atherosclerosis (Lusta et al., 2023; Hansson et al., 2006; Hasham and Pillarisetti, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lusta et al., 2023; Hansson et al., 2006; Hasham and Pillarisetti, 2006.

claim: In healthy arteries, DCs are typically present in the subendothelial space and work in the front line of immune surveillance.
source: In healthy arteries, DCs are typically present in the subendothelial space and work in the front line of immune surveillance (Steinman et al., 2003; Ma-Krupa et al., 2004), and a small portion of resident vascular DCs are localized in the adventitia.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Steinman et al., 2003; Ma-Krupa et al., 2004.

claim: DCs accumulate in advanced atherosclerotic lesions in both humans and animal models.
source: Various studies have demonstrated that DCs accumulate in the advanced atherosclerotic lesions in both humans and animal models (Liu et al., 2008; Jongstra-Bilen et al., 2006; Bobryshev and Lord, 1995; Kawahara et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2008; Jongstra-Bilen et al., 2006; Bobryshev and Lord, 1995; Kawahara et al., 2007.

claim: Several phenotypically and functionally distinct vascular DCs have been identified in mouse and human atherosclerotic lesions.
source: Recently, several phenotypically and functionally distinct vascular DCs have been identified in mouse and human atherosclerotic lesions (Zernecke et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zernecke et al., 2023.

claim: Xcr1+ cDC1 cells are recognized for their role in cross-presentation and activating naive CD8+ T cells, and are critical for anti-viral and anti-tumor immune responses.
source: Xcr1+ type 1 conventional dendritic cells (Xcr1+ cDC1) (also known as CD8+ DC or CD103+ DCs) has been recognized for their role in cross-presentation and activating naive CD8+ T cells, and are critical for anti-viral and anti-tumor immune responses (Eisenbarth, 2019; Bayerl et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Eisenbarth, 2019; Bayerl et al., 2023.

claim: Previous studies investigating the role of cDC1 cells in atherosclerosis using various knockout mice have produced conflicting results.
source: Owing to the challenges associated with obtaining a model for specific cDC1 depletion in vivo, previous studies investigating the role of cDC1 cells in atherosclerosis using various knockout mice have produced conflicting results (Legein et al., 2015; Gil-Pulido et al., 2017; Choi et al., 2011; Clément et al., 2018; Haddad et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Legein et al., 2015; Gil-Pulido et al., 2017; Choi et al., 2011; Clément et al., 2018; Haddad et al., 2017.

claim: Previous Cre lines developed to achieve specific Cre expression in cDC1s led to leakiness in recombinase activity outside of cDC1s.
source: It is important to note that previous Cre lines developed to achieve specific Cre expression in cDC1s still led to leakiness in recombinase activity outside of cDC1s, as demonstrated in previous publications (Wohn et al., 2020; Mundt et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wohn et al., 2020; Mundt et al., 2019.

claim: The major contribution of macrophages in the aortic plaque is recruited from the circulation.
source: Studies have shown that the major contribution of macrophages in the aortic plaque is recruited from the circulation, while other studies have emphasized the significance of local proliferation (Robbins et al., 2013; Potteaux et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Robbins et al., 2013; Potteaux et al., 2011.

claim: Tissue-resident dendritic cells inside atherosclerotic plaques have been well documented.
source: Tissue-resident dendritic cells inside the plaques have been well documented (Yilmaz et al., 2006; Alberts-Grill et al., 2013), regardless of the fact that the contribution and origin of Xcr1+ cDC1 have not been appropriately addressed.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yilmaz et al., 2006; Alberts-Grill et al., 2013.

claim: Xcl1 is a ligand of Xcr1.
source: We further aimed to ascertain whether cDC1 can be modulated by targeting the chemokine Xcl1, which is a ligand of Xcr1.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the Xcl1-Xcr1 interaction.

claim: Xcl1 is the sole receptor for Xcr1.
source: As Xcr1 is the sole receptor for Xcl1, we next explored to target Xcr1+ cDC1 cells via Xcl1 by establishing Xcl1–/–Apoe–/– mice.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the Xcl1-Xcr1 interaction.

claim: Xcl1 serves as a potent chemokine, selectively acting on cDC1 cells through its exclusive receptor, Xcr1.
source: Previous study identified that Xcl1 serves as a potent chemokine, selectively acting on cDC1 cells through its exclusive receptor, Xcr1 (Dorner et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dorner et al., 2009.

claim: Xcr1+ cDC1 cells are crucial for activating T cells in other disease models.
source: In other disease models, Xcr1+ cDC1 cells are crucial for activating T cells (Alexandre et al., 2016; Inui et al., 2023), and we confirmed that in hyperlipidemic mice, the depletion of cDC1 substantially attenuated T cell activation responses.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Alexandre et al., 2016; Inui et al., 2023.

claim: Recent studies have shown Xcr1+ cDC1 cells also engage with CD4+ T cells.
source: It is important to note that Xcr1+ cDC1 cells are known for a well-established role in cross-presentation to CD8+ T cells. Recent studies have shown Xcr1+ cDC1 cells also engage with CD4+ T cells (Wohn et al., 2020; Eickhoff et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wohn et al., 2020; Eickhoff et al., 2015.

claim: Macrophages play a pivotal role in the development and progression of atherosclerotic lesions, particularly within the necrotic core.
source: Given that macrophages play a pivotal role in the development and progression of atherosclerotic lesions, particularly within the necrotic core (De Meyer et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2017), we next investigated macrophage involvement in the aorta using IHC and flow cytometry.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to De Meyer et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2017.

claim: Dyslipidemia is a key characteristic of HFD-treated Apoe–/– mice.
source: Furthermore, since dyslipidemia is a key characteristic of HFD-treated Apoe–/– mice (Piedrahita et al., 1992; Plump et al., 1992), it is critical to assess body weight and lipid profiles in both groups.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Piedrahita et al., 1992; Plump et al., 1992.

claim: Xcl1 is the major chemokine involved in cDC1 recruitment.
source: Xcl1 is the major chemokine involved in cDC1 recruitment (Böttcher et al., 2018; Dorner et al., 2009), and plays a critical role in immune response with diverse physical and pathological implication through its interaction with the sole receptor, Xcr1 (Xu et al., 2019; Yoshida et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Böttcher et al., 2018; Dorner et al., 2009.

claim: Xcl1 plays a critical role in immune response with diverse physical and pathological implications through its interaction with Xcr1.
source: Xcl1 is the major chemokine involved in cDC1 recruitment (Böttcher et al., 2018; Dorner et al., 2009), and plays a critical role in immune response with diverse physical and pathological implication through its interaction with the sole receptor, Xcr1 (Xu et al., 2019; Yoshida et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Xu et al., 2019; Yoshida et al., 1999.

claim: Xcl1 selectively attracts Xcr1+ cDC1 cells in both mice and humans.
source: As Xcr1 is the sole receptor for Xcl1, and Xcl1 selectively attracts Xcr1+ cDC1 cells in both mice and humans (Yoshida et al., 1999; Yoshida et al., 1998), we performed Xcl1 knockout on the background of Apoe–/– mice and assessed the impact on atherosclerosis development.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yoshida et al., 1999; Yoshida et al., 1998.

claim: The Xcl1-Xcr1 axis plays a crucial role in the progression of atherosclerosis.
source: We found that the Xcl1-Xcr1 axis plays a crucial role in the progression of atherosclerosis.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental results showing reduced atherosclerosis in Xcl1 knockout mice.

claim: The loss of Xcl1 in hyperlipidemic Apoe–/– mice significantly reduces atherosclerotic lesion formation.
source: Our results demonstrated that the loss of Xcl1 in hyperlipidemic Apoe–/– mice significantly reduced atherosclerotic lesion formation, decreased the frequencies and absolute counts of Xcr1+ cDC1 cells and CD8+ T cells in the aorta, without affecting lipid status or the number of aortic macrophages.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from Xcl1–/– Apoe–/– mice showing reduced lesion size.

claim: Complete ablation of Xcr1+ cDC1s impairs T cell activation.
source: Notably, while complete ablation of Xcr1+ cDC1s impaired T cell activation, reduction of Xcr1+ cDC1 recruitment via Xcl1 deletion did not significantly compromise this process.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing cDC1-depleted mice with Xcl1 knockout mice.

claim: Reduction of Xcr1+ cDC1 recruitment via Xcl1 deletion does not significantly compromise T cell activation.
source: Notably, while complete ablation of Xcr1+ cDC1s impaired T cell activation, reduction of Xcr1+ cDC1 recruitment via Xcl1 deletion did not significantly compromise this process.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing comparable T cell activation markers in Xcl1 knockout mice.

claim: Alternative chemokine axes may partially rescue Xcr1+ cDC1 homing when Xcl1 is deleted.
source: This discrepancy may arise through compensatory mechanisms: alternative chemokine axes (e.g. CCL5/CCR5, CXCL9/CXCR3, BCL9/BCL9L) may partially rescue Xcr1+ cDC1 homing (Eisenbarth, 2019; de Oliveira et al., 2017; He et al., 2024), while non-cDC1 antigen-presenting cells (e.g. monocytes, cDC2s) may sustain T cell activation (Brewitz et al., 2017; Böttcher et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is speculative and supported by citations to Eisenbarth, 2019; de Oliveira et al., 2017; He et al., 2024.

claim: Non-cDC1 antigen-presenting cells may sustain T cell activation when cDC1 recruitment is reduced.
source: This discrepancy may arise through compensatory mechanisms: alternative chemokine axes (e.g. CCL5/CCR5, CXCL9/CXCR3, BCL9/BCL9L) may partially rescue Xcr1+ cDC1 homing (Eisenbarth, 2019; de Oliveira et al., 2017; He et al., 2024), while non-cDC1 antigen-presenting cells (e.g. monocytes, cDC2s) may sustain T cell activation (Brewitz et al., 2017; Böttcher et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is speculative and supported by citations to Brewitz et al., 2017; Böttcher et al., 2015.

claim: Xcl1 is identified as a potential therapeutic target for atherosclerosis therapy.
source: In summary, our findings identify Xcl1 as a potential therapeutic target for atherosclerosis therapy, though its cellular origins and regulation of lesional Xcr1+ cDC1 and T cells dynamics require further studies.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental results showing reduced atherosclerosis in Xcl1 knockout mice.

claim: Specific depletion of cDC1 attenuates atherosclerosis development by inhibiting both CD4+ and CD8+ T cell activation in hyperlipidemic mice.
source: Here, we established a novel Cre line Xcr1Cre-Gfp mice and did not observe any leakiness of Cre activity, and further experiments revealed that specific depletion of cDC1 attenuates atherosclerosis development by inhibiting both CD4+ and CD8+ T cell activation in hyperlipidemic Xcr1Cre-Gfp Rosa26LSL-DTA Apoe–/– mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from cDC1-depleted mice showing reduced atherosclerosis and decreased T cell activation.

claim: Xcr1+ cDC1 is essential for the development of atherosclerosis.
source: Therefore, our study, which employed genetic models to deplete Xcr1+ cDC1 in vivo in hyperlipidemic mice, has unequivocally determined the essential role of this specific cell type in the development of atherosclerosis.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental results showing reduced atherosclerosis when cDC1 cells are depleted.

claim: Targeting the chemokine Xcl1 can effectively inhibit atherosclerosis.
source: Most importantly, we have successfully demonstrated that targeting the chemokine Xcl1, the ligand of Xcr1, can effectively inhibit atherosclerosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from Xcl1 knockout mice showing reduced atherosclerosis.

claim: Aortic cDC1 cells lack pre-cDC1s and mature cells compared to splenic and lymph node cDC1 cells.
source: As shown in Figure 5, the 10 populations displayed a major difference of aortic cDC1 cells that lack in pre-cDC1s (cluster 10) and mature cells (cluster 3, 7, and 9).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the single-cell RNA sequencing data showing the distribution of cDC1 populations across different organs.

claim: In hyperlipidemic mice, splenic cDC1 possess only Cluster 3 as the late mature cells while lymph node cDC1 cells have two late mature populations, Cluster 3 and Cluster 7.
source: Interestingly, in hyperlipidemic mice splenic cDC1 possess only Cluster 3 as the late mature cells while the lymph node cDC1 cells have two late mature populations, namely Cluster 3 and Cluster 7.
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data showing different mature cDC1 populations in spleen versus lymph nodes.

claim: This novel Cre line is the first of its kind without leakiness of Cre activity under hyperlipidemic conditions.

evidence: The claim is based on the validation experiments showing no Cre activity outside cDC1 cells, and a comparison to previous Cre lines.
